doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: Starting out as an accordionist and discovering arranging
summary: Calello joined a high school band as accordionist and learned harmony on the spot; his musician father pushed the accordion and he found Miles Davis and Gerry Mulligan records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m with Charles Calello today which is a real thrill because you actually did what I wanted to do for a living. I just think that being an arranger is such a creative thing to do, and every week, every day you’re presented with a different issue. Would you agree with that statement?

Yeah well I started to do this as a hobby. I went to the Music & Arts High School and there was really talented, talented players at the age of 13 to 16 years old they were playing on a professional level. And the accordion player in the band, now we’re going back to the ‘50s so the accordion was a common instrument. I was an accordion player. The accordion player in that band got a scholarship to Harvard and they needed an accordion player so I joined the band. And the first rehearsal they said, “Let’s do ‘Almost Like Being in Love.’” So the saxophone player said, “Charlie, give us the notes.” I said, “What do you mean?” He said, “Well play something on the accordion.” So I played [scats]. So he says, “Great,” he says. “All right, give that to the trumpet, now give me a harmony.” I said, “What do you mean?” He said, “Well give me your note that you would play underneath it.” So I gave the – I listened to him and I says, “This is really cool.”
Yeah. And how would you know to play [scats], just that like was inside you from listening to the radio or something?

Well my father was a musician, and I studied trumpet for a while. But my father wanted me to become an accordion player because the accordion players worked at bar mitzvahs and weddings and they always got paid extra because they worked extra hours or something. So my father wanted me to play the accordion. So I had knowledge of music from a very early age and my father, although he played club dates, had Miles Davis records in his collection. So as a kid I found them and I was sort of impressed over the fact that this music was appealing to me. And the first jazz record I heard was Miles – or it was Gerry Mulligan’s arrangement of “Move.” And I studied it and then as I went to high school and started to meet other musicians, I found out that there were people that actually played jazz. And I became interested in it, started to learn chords and things like this. So by the time I got to the band I had some knowledge of what to do. And we were
also writing – in school we were writing figured bass. So I had some knowledge as to, you know, what to do. But these were head arrangements. I wasn’t writing anything out.
